newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila had no choice but to let peso go - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Manila had no choice but to let peso go - analysts.

text.p: The Philippines, running out of currency reserves, had little alternative to Friday's de facto peso devaluation but analysts said it would have saved itself a lot of misery by biting the bullet weeks or months ago.

"They should have done it long ago. If they had had a better policy they would have had a creeping devaluation starting a year ago," said Philippine Institute for Development Studies economist Joseph Yap.
The delay in dealing with the inevitable only makes the pain worse, he said.

After Friday's Central Bank announcement it was finally relaxing its foreign exchange policy, the peso plunged about 11.5 percent against the dollar to its lowest in 45 months at almost 30 pesos to the dollar.
The tumble followed a relentless attack on the peso after the Thai baht's effective devaluation last week and repeated denials by Philippine authorities that they had any intention of following suit.

Even President Fidel Ramos this week raised the spectre of dark forces outside the country deliberately undermining the Philippine peso, after two of his ministers denied using the dread word "devaluation" in interviews with a Singapore newspaper.
Few bankers believed they were telling the truth but many had expected the government to stand by the currency.

The attack on the peso has been building up for weeks as investors worried increasingly that the Philippines was bound to be infected by Thailand's financial crisis, even though the economy was basically in good shape.
A number of economists and Philippine exporters have called for a less stubborn approach to the peso which, until Friday, had barely moved against the dollar in almost two years.

"Based on what we have looked at in the number, because of these two years of pegging the peso at 26.3 to the dollar, the peso had been overvalued very sharply," said Song Seng Wun, regional economist with ABN AMRO Hoare Govett Securities in Singapore.
The Central Bank argument has been that a stable peso meant low inflation and has been able to prove the point after consumer prices by May had fallen to record lows of less than five percent.
That in turn has helped the small but booming economy recover from decades of neglect and mismangement that only really began to change when Ramos took power five years ago.
But the build-up of speculative pressure on the peso was based more on the view that the currency was overpriced rather than that anything was fundamentally wrong with the ecoonmy.
In the end the Philippines simply did not have enough currency reserves to continue to defend the peso against those who were selling their holdings.
Some estimates put Central Bank sales at $2 billion in the past two weeks.

The Bank said its reserves were now only $10 billion, well below the level it wanted, and conceded that it could no longer justify whittling them down further if the market was trying to go in the opposite direction.
Hardest for the private sector were the punitive interest rates set by the Central Bank in the vain hope that they would keep investors with the peso.
But businessmen, at least, were happy with the prospect of lower interest rates and more competitive prices for their exports.
